newsitem.title: USA: Dlr soars vs yen, then trims gains after stocks, bonds fall.
newsitem.headline: Dlr soars vs yen, then trims gains after stocks, bonds fall.

text.p: NEW YORK, Feb 5 - The dollar soared Wednesday to a four-year high against the yen but then trimmed its gains amid a late sell-off in U.S. stocks and bonds.
The yen also weakened versus a broad array of currencies as Japanese investors shifted funds from Japan to more lucrative markets.
The dollar rally began overnight in Tokyo as the Japanese stock market sold off sharply on rumours that Nippon Credit Bank Ltd was having financial difficulties.

Nippon Credit later denied it was having trouble raising funds and said rumours of a collapse were groundless. Many investors, however, remain concerned about the Japanese financial sector because the balance sheets of some banks are full of bad loans.
During Asian trading, the dollar vaulted above 123 yen and continued climbing in New York to 123.85 yen, its highest since it hit 124.33 yen during the week of Feb. 14, 1993.

Helping to fuel the dollar's rally were the British pound's sharp gains against the yen, which some analysts linked to the issuance of corporate bonds denominated in both yen and pounds. The British currency surged above 202 yen for the first time in more than four years.
Japanese investors are keen to buy pounds and other higher-yielding overseas assets because interest rates in Japan remain at rock-bottom levels.

"People are nervous about financial institutions in Japan," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York. "But at the same time, the other concern in the Japanese domestic market is that individuals are divesting from the Japanese domestic market and investing overseas," Yu said. "That's why sterling is also rising."
Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International, said "The dollar's gains against the yen are an indirect result of sterling's gains against the yen, at least today."
In late New York trading on Wednesday, the dollar fetched 123.30 yen, up from 122.40 yen on Tuesday. The dollar slipped to 1.6430 German marks, down from 1.6457 marks.
The British pound rose to $1.6410 from $1.6207.
The dollar fell to 1.4245 Swiss francs from 1.4260 francs, but rose to Canadian $1.3453 from C$1.3443.

The dollar initially strengthened against the mark after a government report indicated that the German economy was still struggling to recover. The German economics ministry reported that west German industrial orders fell 1.4 percent in December and offset a 0.2 percent rise in east German orders.
"It says the German recovery is not proceeding as quickly as had been hoped," McCarthy said. "That helped the dollar out overnight."

Yet by the close of trading in New York, the dollar was lower against the mark and had partially erased its gains against the yen. Traders attributed this partly to a late decline in stocks and bonds.
The Dow Jones industrial average finished down 86.58 points at 6,746.90 and the 30-year Treasury bond fell more than a half point.

"The pressure ... at the end of the day is primarily due to what seems to have been the sudden correction in the direction of the bond market and the stock market after what should have been an uneventful end of the FOMC meeting," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Leumi Trust Co. of New York.
The Federal Open Market Committee left short-term interest rates unchanged, as expected by most economists.
